name: Zinc-air
cathode: Oxygen from ambient air, on a catalyzed carbon electrode
self_discharge: Sealed: 95% of service after 1 year. Activated: about 50% of capacity left after 3 to 12 weeks at 20 °C (Energizer)
summary: Zinc-air cells oxidize a zinc anode with oxygen drawn from the air through holes in the case, giving about 1.4 V and the highest capacity per volume of any miniature battery. They are the common hearing aid battery and lose about half their capacity within 3 to 12 weeks once the seal tab is removed.
body:
## How it works

A zinc-air cell, IEC system P, draws its cathode reactant from the air. The anode is gelled zinc powder in potassium hydroxide electrolyte; the cathode is a thin catalyzed carbon electrode that reduces oxygen taken from the surrounding air. Air enters through a hole in the case, which an adhesive tab seals until use, and a Teflon layer on the cathode lets oxygen in while limiting water loss. Energizer gives the reactions as Zn + 2OH⁻ → ZnO + H2O + 2e⁻ at the anode, O2 + 2H2O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ at the cathode, and 2Zn + O2 → 2ZnO overall.

## Discharge behavior

The reaction has a theoretical voltage of 1.65 V, reduced to about 1.35 to 1.4 V in available cells. Energizer gives a typical operating voltage of 1.4 V that varies with current and depth of discharge, a relatively flat discharge curve and essentially constant internal resistance; its 2026 characteristics table lists 1.45 V nominal. IEC 60086-1 edition 13 lists the system at 1.4 V or 1.45 V nominal. Energizer recommends letting a cell take in air for 30 seconds after removing the tab, and rates continuous use from −10 to 55 °C in its zinc-air manual and −10 to 50 °C in its current characteristics table.

Shelf life depends on the seal. With the tab in place, Energizer reports 95% of initial service after one year and 90% after two. Once activated, a cell retains about 50% of its capacity after 3 to 12 weeks at 20 °C, depending on size, and 0 to 10% beyond 20 weeks. The environment matters: low humidity and high temperature dry the electrolyte, very high humidity floods the cathode, and potassium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide in the air.

## Uses

Energizer describes zinc-air as most effective in applications that use up the cell's capacity within a few weeks, with hearing aids as the typical device. Wikipedia also lists pagers and medical devices, and notes zinc-air as a shorter-lived substitute for discontinued 1.35 V mercury cells.

## History

Wikipedia dates commercial zinc-air products to 1932, with George W. Heise and Erwin A. Schumacher of the National Carbon Company. Thin electrodes developed from fuel-cell research in the 1970s made small button and prismatic cells practical for hearing aids.

## Status

Current. Energizer states that its zinc-air cells contain no added mercury. IEC 60086-1 lists a maximum open-circuit voltage of 1.68 V for system P.
strengths: Highest capacity-to-volume ratio of the miniature systems (Energizer)
Relatively flat discharge and constant internal resistance
Long sealed shelf life: 90% of service after two years with the tab on
limitations: Short life after activation: about 50% capacity left after 3 to 12 weeks
Sensitive to humidity, temperature and carbon dioxide
Needs an air path through the device
safety: Button cell ingestion hazard: swallowed cells can cause severe internal burns
